title: SOLID, part 1
objective: Use three design checks: one reason to change, adding features without editing working code, and subtypes that keep their parent's promises.

sources.title: Robert C. Martin, Solid Relevance (Clean Coder Blog, 2020): one-line definitions of all five SOLID principles
Robert C. Martin, The Open Closed Principle (Clean Coder Blog, 2014), crediting Bertrand Meyer (1988)
Barbara Liskov and Jeannette Wing, A behavioral notion of subtyping (ACM Transactions on Programming Languages and Systems 16(6), 1994)

simplifies: SOLID principles are guidelines for code that will change, not laws. A small script with one shape doesn't need an interface; apply them where change actually happens.

steps.caption: S, single responsibility: "Gather together the things that change for the same reasons." This Report computes figures, lays out a PDF and emails it: three reasons to change.
O, open/closed: "open for extension but closed for modification". AreaCalc breaks it: every new shape edits its if-chain.
Give each shape its own area() behind a Shape interface. A triangle is now a new class; AreaCalc never changes.

predict.prompt: With the Shape interface, what does adding a triangle change?

options.text: Nothing that exists: you add a Triangle class
options.explanation: Right. Open for extension (a new class), closed for modification (AreaCalc stays as it is).
AreaCalc just calls shape.area(); it has no branches any more.
Circle and Square don't know about triangles.

steps.caption: L, Liskov substitution: "A program that uses an interface must not be confused by an implementation of that interface." Square inherits Rectangle, and setting its height also sets its width.
Code written for rectangles is now confused by a Square. Square and Rectangle should both implement Shape rather than one inheriting the other.

predict.prompt: You pass a Square to stretch(). What happens?

options.text: The assert fails: the area is 25
options.explanation: Right. set_height(5) also set the width to 5. Square broke Rectangle's promise that width and height change separately.
For a Rectangle, yes. Square keeps its sides equal, so the width became 5 too.

options.text: Python refuses to pass a Square
options.explanation: A Square is a Rectangle subclass, so Python accepts it.

exercise.change: Add an Ostrich to the bird park (it can't fly either).
exercise.hint: Penguin's fly() raises an error. What did Aviary and Tour have to add so they don't crash?

options.text: Split flying into a Flyer interface; only birds that fly implement it, and Aviary and Tour ask for Flyers
options.explanation: Right. No bird promises something it can't do, so callers need no special cases.
Callers then believe it flew. A silent wrong answer still breaks the promise.

options.text: Add an isinstance check for Ostrich too
options.explanation: That's exactly the edit to avoid: every new non-flyer repeats it in every caller.

exercise.explain: Aviary and Tour no longer check for penguins: they only receive Flyers, and every Flyer can fly. Ostrich is a Bird that isn't a Flyer, so adding it changes nothing that exists.

options.text: You can add behaviour by adding code, without editing code that already works
options.explanation: Right. New shapes, new payment kinds and so on arrive as new classes.
Bugs still get fixed; the principle is about adding features.
It's about design, not file permissions.

quiz.prompt: Square inherits Rectangle, and set_height() also changes the width. Which principle breaks?

options.text: Liskov substitution: code written for Rectangle is surprised by a Square
options.explanation: Right. A subtype must keep its parent's promises.
Square has one job; the trouble is the broken promise.
Nothing here forces edits to working code; the subtype misbehaves.
